{{Short description|Conjecture in abstract algebra about piecewise polynomial functions}}
In [[abstract algebra]], the '''Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture''' asserts that any piecewise-polynomial function can be expressed as a [[Supremum|maximum]] of finite [[Infimum|minima]] of finite collections of [[polynomial]]s. It was first stated, albeit in non-[[Mathematical rigor|rigorous]] and vague wording, in the 1956 paper of [[Garrett Birkhoff]] and [[Richard S. Pierce]] in which they first introduced [[f-ring]]s. The modern, rigorous statement of the conjecture was formulated by [[Melvin Henriksen]] and [[John R. Isbell]], who worked on the problem in the early 1960s in connection with their work on f-rings. Their formulation is as follows:

:For every real piecewise-polynomial function <math>f \colon \R^n \rightarrow \R</math>, [[there exists]] a finite set of polynomials <math>g_{ij} \in \R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]</math> such that <math>f = \sup_i \inf_j ( g_{ij} )</math>.<ref name="Lucas">{{cite journal| last1 = Lucas | first1 = François|first2=James J.|last2= Madden |first3=Daniel |last3=Schaub |first4=Mark |last4=Spivakovsky  | year = 2009 | title = On connectedness of sets in the real spectra of polynomial rings | journal = Manuscripta Mathematica | volume = 128 | pages = 505–547 | doi = 10.1007/s00229-008-0244-1 | issue = 4| arxiv = math/0601671|mr=2487439 }}</ref>

Isbell is likely the source of the name ''Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture'', and popularized the problem in the 1980s by discussing it with several mathematicians interested in [[real algebraic geometry]].<ref name="Lucas"/>

The conjecture was proved true for ''n'' = 1 and 2 by [[Louis Mahé]].<ref>{{cite web | title=The Pierce–Birkhoff Conjecture | publisher=Atlas Conferences, Inc. | url=http://atlas-conferences.com/c/a/c/v/66.htm | date=1999-07-05 | url-status=dead | archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110608074427/http://atlas-conferences.com/c/a/c/v/66.htm | archivedate=2011-06-08 }}</ref>

== Local Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture ==
In 1989, [[James J. Madden]] provided an equivalent statement that is in terms of the [[real spectrum]] of <math>A = R[x_1, \ldots, x_n]</math> and the novel concepts of local polynomial representatives and separating ideals.

Denoting the real spectrum of ''A'' by <math>\operatorname{Sper} A</math>, the ''separating ideal of ''α'' and ''β in <math>\operatorname{Sper} A</math> is the ideal of ''A'' generated by all polynomials <math>g \in A</math> that change sign on <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>, i.e., <math>g(\alpha) \ge 0</math> and <math>g(\beta) \le 0</math>. Any finite covering <math>\R^n = \bigcup_i P_i</math> of [[Closed set|closed]], [[semi-algebraic set]]s induces a corresponding covering <math>\operatorname{Sper} A = \bigcup_i\tilde{P}_i</math>, so, in particular, when ''f'' is piecewise polynomial, there is a polynomial <math>f_i</math> for every <math>\alpha\in\operatorname{Sper} A</math> such that <math>f|_{P_i} = f_i|_{P_i}</math> and <math>\alpha\in\tilde{P}_i</math>. This <math>f_i</math> is termed the ''local polynomial representative of ''f'' at <math>\alpha</math>.''

Madden's so-called ''local Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture'' at <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>, which is equivalent to the Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture, is as follows:
: Let <math>\alpha</math>, <math>\beta</math> be in <math>\operatorname{Sper} A</math> and ''f'' be piecewise-polynomial. It is conjectured that for every local representative of ''f'' at <math>\alpha</math>, <math>f_\alpha</math>, and local representative of ''f'' at <math>\beta</math>, <math>f_\beta</math>, <math>f_\alpha - f_\beta</math> is in the separating ideal of <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>.<ref name="Lucas"/>
